summary: Alberta lookout in our records; no public source found describes this tower, its build date, staffing or current use.

evidence.supports: Alberta publishes a map of its wildfire lookout sites, 127 in number, across the boreal forest and along the Rocky Mountains
evidence.quote: Map showing the locations of Alberta's 127 wildfire lookout sites, which are situated throughout the province's boreal forest and along the Rocky Mountains.

evidence.supports: the province says lookouts are sited where visibility is good for detecting and reporting wildfires
evidence.quote: are located where visibility is favourable to detect and report wildfires

evidence.supports: early lookouts were often trees with branches removed, used to support bush ladders
evidence.quote: trees with their branches removed serving as supports for bush ladders

evidence.supports: steel began to replace wood for tower construction in the 1920s
evidence.quote: Introduced in the 1920s, steel increasingly replaced wood for tower construction.

evidence.supports: in 1945 lookouts adopted the Osborne, an instrument that helps locate a fire from the tower
evidence.quote: Then in 1945, lookouts adopted the Osborne, an instrument used to help determine the precise location of a fire in relation to the tower.

evidence.supports: many operational lookouts were rebuilt on the site of the first ones
evidence.quote: Many of Alberta’s 127 operational fire lookouts are rebuilt on the location of the first generation of lookouts.

evidence.supports: Alberta Wildfire's blog describes lookout observers as the forestry service's eyes and ears across the alpine, foothills and boreal regions
evidence.quote: Lookout observers are forestry’s eyes and ears in the alpine, foothills, and boreal regions of Alberta.

evidence.supports: the blog is posted by Alberta Wildfire

sources.title: Firefighter in the Field: An Office in the Sky

notes_for_editor: PROTECTED DATA: the built year (2015), height (30 m), access mode (fly) and the staffing and access note in the tower record come only from the Alberta Wildfire WF_WILDFIRE_LOOKOUT layer. Its metadata says it is classed Protected and not to be displayed on maps the general public will see. I kept those values out of the story and facts. Decide before publishing them. NO SITE SOURCE: two searches and several reads found nothing public about this lookout by name, and the 2009 cached Alberta lookout map (data/raw/expansion/prairies-north/ab_lookout_map_2009.txt, public URL not recorded) appears to carry GORDON and LAKE as split labels, so it may show an earlier site there than the 2015 structure. The Canada Lookouts Alberta index (cached only) links a GORDON LAKE page, but that subpage is 404 live and its cached copy has no body text, so nothing can be cited from it. A firelookout.org Alberta list (2008) is reported as having no Gordon entry, but that page is also unreadable (404), so it is not used. The record's access note (staffed March to October, please do not visit) has no public source and is left out. No photos found. The story is generic context plus an honest gap; consider holding it until a site-specific source turns up.
